variants.title: Turn a battle into data
variants.context: A battle is one prompt, two comparable model runs, one randomized presentation, and one recorded judgment. The pipeline has to preserve that contract before any aggregation can be trusted.
variants.prompt: An internal arena is being built from scratch. Put the stages of one battle in order.

items.text: Generate comparably: use the same prompt and disclose material differences in system instructions, tools, temperature, token limits, and latency policy.
Filter and estimate: remove invalid events with auditable rules, aggregate pairwise outcomes, bootstrap uncertainty, and publish slice diagnostics.
Sample a prompt and a pair: choose a prompt slice and two eligible models, tracking pair coverage so available models do not dominate.
Randomize and collect: hide identity, swap left and right placement, permit ties or both-bad outcomes, and retain the assignment metadata.

variants.hint: Which stage is the only one allowed to see a model identity?
variants.explanation: Identity stays hidden until after the vote, and filtering and estimation happen offline after the immutable event is recorded.

variants.title: Turn a battle into data
variants.context: A battle is one prompt, two comparable model runs, one randomized presentation, and one recorded judgment. The pipeline has to preserve that contract before any aggregation can be trusted.
variants.prompt: An architect draws the arena data path end to end. Put the components in order.

items.text: The pair scheduler balances exposure across models and opponents.
The immutable event log stores assignment, outcome, and quality metadata.
The blind voting UI collects a choice with randomized positions and no visible model identity.
The generation gateway runs both models and captures versions, settings, errors, latency, and cost.
The prompt sampler assigns a documented slice and applies eligibility rules.
The analysis pipeline filters, aggregates, bootstraps, slices, and publishes.

variants.hint: Keep the online path small and push the statistics offline.
variants.explanation: Filtering, fitting, bootstrapping, and slice reporting belong in reproducible offline jobs, not in the live battle path.

variants.title: Turn a battle into data
variants.context: A battle is one prompt, two comparable model runs, one randomized presentation, and one recorded judgment. The pipeline has to preserve that contract before any aggregation can be trusted.
variants.prompt: An analyst must reproduce one published estimate six months later. Put the steps in order that make that possible.

items.text: Record the left and right assignment along with the vote outcome, including tie and both-bad options.
Recompute the aggregate and interval from the raw log under the recorded filter version.
Record the sampled prompt, its slice, and the eligibility rules that allowed this model pair.
Apply exclusions as a separate versioned filter decision rather than deleting events.
Append the event to the raw log without editing it.
Record both model versions and generation configurations from the gateway.

variants.hint: What has to stay untouched for the recomputation to mean anything?
variants.explanation: Raw votes are append-only, and corrections and exclusions are separate versioned decisions, which is what lets an old analysis be reproduced.

variants.title: Apply the decision rule
variants.context: A leaderboard is an input to investigation, not a release gate. The operational rule checks diagnostics, then the interval against a predeclared practical threshold, then slice agreement, then separate correctness, safety, latency, cost, and policy gates, before a bounded canary.
variants.prompt: A candidate model tops the internal arena and the team wants to act on it. Put the operational decision rule in order.

items.text: Verify that important prompt and user slices agree, or explain the disagreement.
Check whether the preference interval clears a predeclared practical threshold, not merely 50 percent.
Record the data window, model versions, estimator, filters, and decision owner.
Begin a bounded canary with rollback thresholds.
Require separate correctness, safety, latency, cost, and policy gates to pass.
Confirm that assignment and quality-control diagnostics are healthy.

variants.hint: The first check is about the evaluation system, not the candidate.
variants.explanation: A preference lead only earns the next check; correctness, safety, latency, cost, and policy remain separate gates before any exposure.

variants.title: Apply the decision rule
variants.context: A leaderboard is an input to investigation, not a release gate. The operational rule checks diagnostics, then the interval against a predeclared practical threshold, then slice agreement, then separate correctness, safety, latency, cost, and policy gates, before a bounded canary.
variants.prompt: The candidate leads at 53 percent, but the interval runs from 50.4 to 55.6 and the practical threshold is 52. Put the response in order.

items.text: Record the data window, model versions, estimator, and filters with the hold decision.
Compare the interval against the predeclared practical threshold rather than against 50 percent.
Confirm that left and right balance, pair coverage, and filter reasons look healthy.
Hold the release instead of ranking on the point estimate.
Observe that the lower bound sits below the threshold, so the lead is not practically supported.

variants.hint: Which number does the threshold apply to, the estimate or the bound?
variants.explanation: Clearing 50 percent is not the bar; the interval has to clear the practical threshold that was declared before the leaderboard was read.

variants.title: Apply the decision rule
variants.context: A leaderboard is an input to investigation, not a release gate. The operational rule checks diagnostics, then the interval against a predeclared practical threshold, then slice agreement, then separate correctness, safety, latency, cost, and policy gates, before a bounded canary.
variants.prompt: The aggregate favors the candidate, but the Spanish-language slice reverses the result. Put the response in order.

items.text: Require the separate correctness, safety, latency, cost, and policy gates to pass.
Start a bounded canary limited to the slices that agree, with rollback thresholds.
Investigate the disagreeing slice and either explain it or publish the slice result beside the aggregate.
Check that the aggregate interval clears the predeclared practical threshold.
Confirm the diagnostics are healthy so the disagreement is not an assignment artifact.

variants.hint: A disagreeing slice is evidence, not noise to average away.
variants.explanation: Publish the traffic-weighted result and the important slice results together; an unexplained slice reversal narrows the claim rather than disappearing into the aggregate.

variants.title: Size the battle budget
variants.context: Arena capacity is driven by battles, but every battle costs two generations and yields at most one usable vote. Skipped, invalid, and filtered battles still consume serving capacity.
variants.prompt: An internal arena records 15,000 battles per day and each response averages 600 output tokens. How many output tokens per day does the serving path emit before retries?
variants.explanation: Each battle needs two generations, so 15,000 times 2 times 600 is 18 million output tokens per day.

mistakes.feedback: That counts one generation per battle; a battle serves two responses before it can produce a vote.
That is off by a factor of ten in the conversion to millions; 18,000,000 tokens is 18 million.

variants.title: Size the battle budget
variants.context: Arena capacity is driven by battles, but every battle costs two generations and yields at most one usable vote. Skipped, invalid, and filtered battles still consume serving capacity.
variants.prompt: An arena has a daily budget of 24 million output tokens and responses average 400 tokens. How many battles per day can it serve before retries?
variants.hint: What does one battle cost in output tokens?
variants.explanation: One battle costs two responses of 400 tokens, so 24,000,000 divided by 800 is 30,000 battles per day.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by one response instead of two; every battle serves two generations.
That divides by 1,600 tokens, which is four responses; a battle has two.

variants.title: Size the battle budget
variants.context: Arena capacity is driven by battles, but every battle costs two generations and yields at most one usable vote. Skipped, invalid, and filtered battles still consume serving capacity.
variants.prompt: An arena records 20,000 battles per day at 400 output tokens per response, and 20 percent of battles are skipped, invalid, or filtered. How many output tokens are spent per usable vote?
variants.hint: Filtered battles still cost their generations.
variants.explanation: The path emits 16,000,000 output tokens and yields 16,000 usable votes, so each usable vote costs 1,000 tokens.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by all 20,000 battles; only 16,000 of them produced a usable vote.
That counts one generation per battle instead of the two every battle actually serves.

variants.title: Defend the analysis choice
variants.context: Every analysis choice encodes a trade-off, so it is declared before the leaderboard is read and then tested for sensitivity. Scheduling probabilities, resampling units, and tie rules all change what the estimate means.
variants.prompt: The scheduler switches from uniform random pairing to adaptive pairing that concentrates battles near uncertain boundaries. What must the analysis do?
options: Log the changing selection probabilities and account for them in the estimator.
Keep the previous estimator, because adaptive pairing only changes which battles are run.
Discard the adaptive battles and fit only on the uniformly sampled ones.
optionFeedback: Correct: the scheduler is part of the statistical design, so its selection probabilities have to be logged and handled.
Which battles are run is exactly what changes the estimator's assumptions about the sample.
Throwing away the adaptive battles wastes the evidence that was collected where it mattered most.
variants.hint: Is the scheduler outside the statistics, or part of them?
variants.explanation: Adaptive pairing concentrates evidence near uncertain boundaries, but its changing selection probabilities must be logged and handled in analysis.

variants.title: Defend the analysis choice
variants.context: Every analysis choice encodes a trade-off, so it is declared before the leaderboard is read and then tested for sensitivity. Scheduling probabilities, resampling units, and tie rules all change what the estimate means.
variants.prompt: One voter cast 400 of the 3,000 votes in the reporting window. Which resampling unit should the bootstrap use?
options: Resample individual votes, because each vote is one independent observation.
Resample by model pair, because the estimate is about the matchup.
Resample by voter or session, because that is where the dependence lives.
optionFeedback: Many related votes from one person are not independent, so this understates the uncertainty.
The pair is what is being estimated, not the unit of correlated sampling.
Correct: bootstrap by an independent unit that matches the dependence, which here is the voter or session.
variants.hint: Which unit could repeat its own preferences hundreds of times?
variants.explanation: Resampling individual votes when one person casts many related votes understates uncertainty, so the resampling unit has to match the clustering.

variants.title: Defend the analysis choice
variants.context: Every analysis choice encodes a trade-off, so it is declared before the leaderboard is read and then tested for sensitivity. Scheduling probabilities, resampling units, and tie rules all change what the estimate means.
variants.prompt: The candidate leads when ties are split evenly but trails when ties are excluded. What is the defensible report?
options: Report the matchup as tie-rule dependent and publish both rules with the tie rate.
Report the split-tie result, since splitting ties is the standard convention.
Report the tie-excluded result, since ties carry no preference information.
optionFeedback: Correct: tie sensitivity reveals that the conclusion depends on counting ambiguous outcomes one particular way.
A convention does not resolve a conclusion that flips when the convention changes.
Excluding ties throws away the ambiguity that is itself the finding here.
variants.hint: What is the finding when two valid rules disagree?
variants.explanation: Tie handling is a declared decision, and a conclusion that reverses under a different tie rule is reported as unresolved rather than as a rank.

variants.title: Diagnose the bias
variants.context: Sampling uncertainty is variation from a finite number of votes. Systematic bias is a repeatable shift caused by the evaluation design. More votes shrink the first and leave the second exactly where it was.
variants.prompt: Match each named failure mode to what it does to the estimate.

pairs.label: Position and presentation bias
pairs.detail: Voters favor one side of the screen, shifting the estimate toward whichever model appears there more often.

pairs.label: Prompt-selection bias
pairs.detail: The sampled languages, domains, difficulty, and intents do not match the traffic the result is applied to.

pairs.label: Voter-selection bias
pairs.detail: Who was recruited to vote, and how, does not represent the population the claim is made about.

pairs.label: Pairing and availability bias
pairs.detail: The scheduler exposes some models to easier opponents, so quality and scheduling get confused.

variants.hint: Ask which part of the design does the shifting: the screen, the prompts, the people, or the scheduler.
variants.explanation: Each of these is a repeatable shift caused by the evaluation design, which is why collecting more votes narrows the interval around the wrong value.

variants.title: Diagnose the bias
variants.context: Sampling uncertainty is variation from a finite number of votes. Systematic bias is a repeatable shift caused by the evaluation design. More votes shrink the first and leave the second exactly where it was.
variants.prompt: Match each observed symptom to the failure mode it points at.

pairs.label: Left responses win 56 percent of battles across every model
pairs.detail: Position and presentation bias, tested by randomizing placement per battle.

pairs.label: The winner is the most verbose and heavily formatted model on factual prompts
pairs.detail: Style over substance, tested by adding correctness and citation checks.

pairs.label: A handful of sessions account for most votes in one matchup
pairs.detail: Abuse and correlated votes, tested by rate limits and coordinated-pattern detection.

pairs.label: One model faces far weaker opponents than the others
pairs.detail: Pairing and availability bias, tested by monitoring pair coverage and error rates.

variants.hint: Read the symptom as a question about which control was missing.
variants.explanation: Every bias has a specific diagnostic; naming the symptom is only useful if it points at the control that should have caught it.

variants.title: Diagnose the bias
variants.context: Sampling uncertainty is variation from a finite number of votes. Systematic bias is a repeatable shift caused by the evaluation design. More votes shrink the first and leave the second exactly where it was.
variants.prompt: Match each control to the thing it protects the estimate from.

pairs.label: Randomize left and right placement independently for each valid battle
pairs.detail: A stable screen-side preference silently shifting the score.

pairs.label: Publish traffic-weighted results beside important slice results
pairs.detail: One dominant prompt slice standing in for languages, domains, and intents it does not represent.

pairs.label: State who voted and how they were recruited
pairs.detail: A public volunteer sample being generalized to a specialized workforce without validation.

pairs.label: Version filters and report how exclusions change the estimate
pairs.detail: An unauditable cleanup step quietly deciding the outcome.

variants.hint: Work backwards from the control to the failure it exists to catch.
variants.explanation: Controls are only credible when the report says what they were protecting against and what happened when they were varied.
